high variable gene symbols present in our evaluated datasets. This input design may introduce performance
variabilies compared to other models.
Moreover, to support users in making informed decisions about which foundation models to use,
we
provided a Model Recommendation Guide (Supplementary Table 5). This guide summarizes the best-
performing FMs across four evaluation settings: (1) pooled-data with layer-freezing, (2) pooled-data with fine-
tuning, (3) cross-data with layer-freezing, and (4) cross-data with fine-tuning. By linking model performance
to evaluation scenario, tissue type, drug class, and cancer type, the guide offers a practical framework for
selecting or adapting models to specific research contexts. Overall, scFoundation and scGPT emerge as strong
default choices for pooled-data applications across most tissues, drug classes, and cancer types. In contrast,
cross-data scenarios require more careful consideration, as performance tends to be more variable. In these
cases, models such as UCE, tGPT, and other task-specific architectures often demonstrate stronger
generalization. Finally, for rare cancers or highly imbalanced datasets, we recommend that researchers place
particular emphasis on cross-data performance, since not all models are equally reliable under such
challenging conditions.
5. Validation datasets seem to have been used in a non-standard way. My understanding is that usually the
validation datasets should be held out and not used in training at all. However, the authors have performed a
train-test split on the validation datasets to train models, independently of models already trained-tested on
the primary data. Is there a particular reason for such a choice?
Response: Thanks for the comments. We would like to clarify the rationale behind our use of the primary and
validation datasets. The primary data collection was assembled at the initial stage of this benchmarking study
and served as the foundation for our main analyses. As additional datasets became available, we then
assembled a validation data collection. This independent collection was intended not only to confirm the
findings obtained from the primary data, but also to broaden the evaluation to a more diverse range of tissues,
diseases, and experimental conditions. In this way, the validation datasets serve as an additional and more
stringent test of model generalizability beyond the original data pool.
To maintain fairness and consistency, we applied the same benchmarking strategy to the validation data as
was used for the primary data, performing a train-test split within each dataset and evaluating the foundation
models independently of those trained on the primary collection. This ensured that all models were compared
under similar conditions while still being tested on unseen data partitions.
Importantly, to further evaluate the model generalizability, we also evaluated the models on the validation
datasets in a zero-shot learning setting without any additional training. These results, reported in the
Supplementary Note 11, demonstrate that the models can directly predict drug response labels on entirely
independent data. Together, the two analyses, train-test split and zero-shot evaluation, provide a more
comprehensive and rigorous assessment of model performance.
In summary, the validation datasets were designed to serve a dual role: first, to confirm reproducibility of
results obtained from the primary data; and second, to expand the evaluation to newly emerging and more
diverse datasets. We believe this approach strengthens the conclusions of the study by giving readers a clearer
picture of model generalizability across independent data sources.
Minor comments
1. While F1 and AUROC are relevant metrics, the authors should consider reporting Pearson/Sprearman
correlations between known and predicted responses as well.
Response: Thanks for the comments. In the revised manuscript, we reported the Pearson correlations between
known and predicted responses, using results from the pooled-data evaluation in the primary dataset, with
models fine-tuned using LoRA. We examined datasets spanning multiple tissue types, drug classes, cancer
types, and treatment regimens.
Our results show that scFoundation consistently achieved better correlations between predicted and ground-
truth responses. For example, it obtained Pearson correlations of 0.8437 in tumor tissue, 0.8915 in acute
lymphoblastic leukemia, 0.8652 in targeted therapy, and 0.8984 in the anti-CD19 CAR-T regimen
(Supplementary Table 3; Supplementary Fig. 13). Other models, such as scGPT, CellPLM, tGPT, and
Geneformer, also demonstrated competitive performance across several settings. For instance, in tumor tissue,
their mean correlation scores were 0.7289, 0.6156, 0.5925, and 0.5923, respectively. In contrast, UCE,
scBERT, and CellLM generally did not perform very well (Supplementary Table 3; Supplementary Fig.
13). These results indicate that while fine-tuned foundation models vary in their ability to preserve predictive
signal across datasets, scFoundation shows consistently superior performance, suggesting its robustness in
aligning predictions with true drug response outcomes (Supplementary Note 4; Supplementary Table 3;
Supplementary Fig. 13).
2. In figure 3, since two methods are being compared, it would make sense for AUROC plots to either both
be violin plots or box plots.
Response: Thanks for the comments. In the revised Fig. 3, we have updated the AUROC plot to box plots.
3. A case study or an example of a drug response predicted by the best performing model would be an
interesting addition to the paper.
Response: Thanks for the comments. In the revised manuscript, we added a case study of drug response
predictions generated by the best-performing models. To illustrate the potential impact of inaccurate
predictions, we analyzed Data 3 (Supplementary Tables 1–2) and compared biological insights derived from
ground truth labels with those obtained from scGPT-predicted labels (Supplementary Note 5;
Supplementary Figs. 14–17). In Data 3, ground-truth annotations indicated 10,897 resistant cells (67.95%)
and 5,140 sensitive cells (32.05%), whereas scGPT predicted 62.95% resistant and 37.05% sensitive, showing
noticeable shifts in response proportions that may alter downstream biological interpretations.
For our analysis, we used Seurat for dimensionality reduction and clustering, followed by manual
annotation of cell populations based on canonical marker genes. This yielded 16,037 tumor cells, 4,923 CD8⁺
T cells, 1,157 CD4⁺ T cells, 6,077 monocytes/macrophages, 3,355 natural killer (NK) cells, 519 dendritic cells,
325 progenitors, 360 erythrocytes, and 3,117 B cells (Supplementary Fig. 14). We then conducted several
downstream analyses including differentially expressed genes identification; over-representation enrichment
analysis using GO (Gene Ontology), KEGG (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes), and MSigDB
Hallmark gene sets; cell-cell interaction inference; and pseudotime trajectory analysis. Our results revealed
that several key biological findings were only recovered when using ground-truth labels, but were missed
when relying on predicted labels. For example, ground-truth based analysis identified COL1A2 and SEZ6L2
as top up-regulated genes in resistant tumor cells and highlighted enrichment of biological processes such as
cell differentiation, cell-cell adhesion, and the p53 pathway (Supplementary Note 5; Supplementary Fig.
14, Supplementary Fig. 16). In addition, stronger intercellular communication was observed in dendritic cells
and B cells as receivers in resistant tumor cells, while weaker BTLA and CD160 signalling was detected in
CD8⁺ T cells, NK cells, dendritic cells, progenitors, and B cells (Supplementary Note 5; Supplementary
Figs. 15, Supplementary Fig. 17). Furthermore, the ground-truth labels revealed a coherent pseudotime
trajectory from sensitive to resistant states (Supplementary Note 5; Supplementary Figs. 15,
Supplementary Fig. 17). These discrepancies highlight the importance of ensuring high prediction accuracy
to enable more reliable and meaningful biomechanistic insights for drug discovery.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
This manuscript presents scDrugMap, a comprehensive benchmarking framework for evaluating 10
foundation models (8 single-cell-specific, 2 general LLMs) in predicting drug response from single-cell
transcriptomics. The study curates 345,607 cells across 53 datasets spanning 14 cancer types, 3 therapies, and
5 tissues. The authors demonstrated that scFoundation dominates pooled-data prediction, while UCE and
scGPT lead in cross-data generalization; fine-tuning universally outperforms layer-freezing, general LLMs
(e.g., GPT4o-mini) fail in zero-shot tasks, and computational efficiency varies sharply (scFoundation ≫
scGPT).
In the context of growing tumor single-cell data and proliferating LLMs, scDrugMap establishes the first
benchmark for foundation models in drug response prediction. It validates specialized single-cell FMs over
general LLMs for clinical reliability, provides scenario-specific model selection guidelines, and quantifies
computational trade-offs—directly enabling more accurate, deployable treatment response prediction in
precision oncology. The study's claims of novelty are undermined by its exclusive reliance on existing models
without algorithmic innovation, and its benchmarking framework closely mirrors prior approaches. Data
integration lacks originality, repurposing public GEO datasets without novel experimental validation.
Crucially, the work fails to cite key literature (e.g., GPTCelltype for LLM benchmarking; DREEP for drug
response prediction), overstating its "first comprehensive benchmark" contribution while overlooking
established methodologies in adjacent domains.
Major Concerns:
1. Questionable novelty. All models are repurposed (scGPT, Geneformer). Fails to cite comparable
benchmarks (e.g., GPTCelltype, Nat Methods 2024). Positions as "first" without literature context.
Response: Thanks for the comments. We agree that many of the foundation models included in our benchmark,
such as scGPT and Geneformer, were originally developed for broader single-cell analysis tasks. Our
contribution lies in systematically repurposing and benchmarking these models specifically for drug response
prediction, a problem of critical importance in cancer treatment but one that has not yet been rigorously
evaluated across diverse single-cell datasets.
In the revised manuscript, we now cite and discuss relevant comparable work, including GPTCelltype (Nat
Methods, 2024), which highlighted the utility of GPT-4 for cell type annotation in scRNA-seq data. As noted
in our manuscript (lines 69–76, these foundation models have indeed been applied to a variety of tasks,
including cell type annotation, batch effect removal, multi-omics integration, gene dosage sensitivity
prediction, and chromatin dynamics modeling. While scFoundation has been tested for drug response
prediction in a limited context, no prior study has performed a comprehensive, systematic benchmark of
multiple large-scale single-cell foundation models for this specific task.
Our work addresses this gap by providing the first unified evaluation framework, along with a large and
diverse collection of drug response-related single-cell datasets, to rigorously compare foundation models
under both pooled-data and cross-data scenarios, across multiple cancer types, tissues, and therapeutic
regimens. By focusing explicitly on drug resistance prediction, we not only highlight the strengths and
weaknesses of existing models in this domain but also provide practical guidance for selecting models in
biomedical and translational research. We believe this represents a meaningful advance beyond simply
repurposing existing models, as it delivers a new benchmarking resource tailored to one of the most pressing
challenges in precision oncology.
2. Lack of baseline comparisons. The study does not include comparisons with established non–foundation
model (non-FM) methods such as DREEP or scDEAL, which limits the ability to assess the added value of
the proposed foundation models. Without such benchmarks, it remains unclear whether the FMs truly offer
performance improvements. If the FMs underperform relative to these simpler or more established approaches,
the core premise of the study—that foundation models provide superior predictive power—would be
significantly weakened.
Response: Thanks for the comments. In our revision, we included baseline comparisons with three established
non–foundation model (non-FM) methods: a multilayer perceptron (MLP), scDEAL (a deep learning
framework for drug response prediction at the single-cell level), and DREEP (a statistical method for drug
response estimation from single-cell transcriptional profiles of tumors). These non-FM baselines were
systematically evaluated under both cross-dataset and pooled-dataset scenarios (Supplementary Note 3;
Supplementary Figs. 11–12).
Our results show that, overall, non-FM methods did not outperform foundation models. Interestingly, among
the non-FMs, the MLP trained on pooled data achieved strong and consistent results than scDEAL and DREEP
in several contexts, including targeted therapy, cell line data, and cancer datasets such as melanoma (F1 =
0.875 ± 0.0014), breast cancer (0.774 ± 0.0038), and lung cancer (0.737 ± 0.0041). In some cases, such as
liver cancer, scDEAL, DREEP, and MLP achieved performance equivalent to several foundation models (e.g.,
mean F1 = 0.924). However, across the broader evaluation landscape, particularly in cross-data scenarios
where generalization is critical, foundation models consistently demonstrated superior predictive power
compared with non-FMs. This highlights one of the central advantages of pre-trained FMs, i.e., their ability
to transfer learned representations and maintain performance across heterogeneous datasets, which is
especially important for drug response prediction in diverse cancer contexts.
In summary, while non-FM baselines can occasionally perform well under pooled-data conditions, our
systematic comparisons show that foundation models provide more robust and generalizable predictive
performance, thereby reinforcing their value for single-cell drug response prediction.
3. Overinterpretation of marginal results. UCE’s "top" cross-data performance (F1=0.774) is clinically
irrelevant. Claiming it "achieves optimal results" (Fig 3b) misrepresents data. Similarly, scFoundation’s
failure in PBMCs (F1=0.461) is glossed over.
Response: Thanks for the comments. We have carefully revised the manuscript to clarify and moderate our
interpretation.
Specifically, we have removed any language that could be construed as overstating UCE’s performance. In
the main text, the previous description of UCE as a “top” performer has been replaced with the more accurate:
“UCE demonstrated relatively stronger performance compared to other models across various categories,
despite the overall modest performance observed across all models” (lines 211–213). Moreover, in the abstract
(lines 30-31), we revised the phrase “achieves optimal results” to the more precise: “UCE for tumor tissue
showed relatively better performance (mean F1 score: 0.774)”. Finally, regarding the F1 = 0.461, we would
like to clarify that this result corresponds to CellLM, not scFoundation, under the layer-freezing pooled-data
evaluation scenario. As stated in the manuscript (lines 152–153): “CellLM and scBERT underperformed on
PBMCs data (mean F1 scores: 0.461 and 0.483, respectively). In contrast, scFoundation performed well on
PBMCs in the same scenario, achieving a mean F1 score of 0.939, ranking highest among all models (Fig.
2a).” Moreover, across our benchmarks, CellLM consistently showed limited performance, with its best result
observed in acute lymphoblastic leukemia under cross-data evaluation with full fine-tuning (mean F1 = 0.718;
Supplementary Fig. 3). Taken together, these revisions ensure our interpretations are appropriately cautious,
accurately represent the results, and avoid overstatement of model performance.
4. Data biases compromise conclusions. Severe class imbalance (e.g., 86% resistant cells in neuroblastoma;
Supp Table 2) inflates F1 scores. AUPRC should supplement F1 for imbalanced subgroups. Batch effects
across 36 datasets are ignored. No correction (e.g., Harmony) was applied, invalidating cross-dataset claims.
Response: Thanks for the comments. In our revised manuscript, we investigated the issue of class imbalance
and the potential impact of batch effects.
Class imbalance. According to Supplementary Table 2, the neuroblastoma dataset (Data13) consists of
5,492 sensitive cells (46.58%) and 6,298 resistant cells (53.42%), which does not show severe imbalance.
That said, we agree that class imbalance is a concern in certain datasets. For this study, we defined severe
imbalance as cases where one class exceeds 70% of the total. Based on this criterion, two datasets in our
primary collection are imbalanced: Data 23 (lung cancer; 15.51% sensitive vs. 84.49% resistant) and Data 32
(prostate cancer; 20.15% sensitive vs. 79.85% resistant). To account for this, we supplemented F1 with
AUPRC, which is more appropriate for imbalanced data. Using fine-tuned models with LoRA under both
pooled-data and cross-data scenarios, we found that pooled-data evaluations consistently outperformed cross-
data ones. For instance, in Data 23, scFoundation (AUPRC = 0.894), scGPT (AUPRC = 0.802), and CellPLM
(AUPRC = 0.709) all achieved strong predictive performance above 0.7, despite the imbalance. Similarly, in
Data 32, pooled-data training again yielded stronger results, with scFoundation (AUPRC = 0.747), scGPT
(AUPRC = 0.619), and CellPLM (AUPRC = 0.518) ranking highest (Supplementary Note 9;
Supplementary Fig. 22). These findings show that for severe imbalanced datasets (e.g. resistant cell
proportion exceeding 70%), models under pooled-data evaluation consistently outperformed those in cross-
data scenarios. Among these, scFoundation, scGPT, and CellPLM generally achieved better predictive
performance than other models.
Batch effects. To address the concern about batch effects across diverse datasets, we applied Harmony on the
top 2000 highly variable genes in each dataset for batch correction (Supplementary Note 2; Supplementary
Fig. 7-8). With the batch corrected data, we again conducted comprehensive benchmarking under two
evaluation scenarios: pooled-data evaluation (Supplementary Fig. 7) and cross-data evaluation
(Supplementary Fig. 8). In both settings, we also implemented two model training strategies (layer freezing
and fine-tuning using LoRA). Our results showed that performance with batch correction was largely
consistent with the results obtained without correction. Top-performing models such as scFoundation, scGPT,
and CellPLM remained stable or exhibited only minor improvements after batch correction (Supplementary
Fig. 7a). For example, in tumor tissue, the F1 scores with and without batch correction were: scFoundation =
0.998 vs. 0.998; scGPT = 0.939 vs. 0.939; and CellPLM = 0.940 vs. 0.936. This phenomynon is also observed
in other models, such as tGPT, Geneformer, and UCE, exhibited comparable performance before and after
batch correction. For instance, in targeted therapy datasets, tGPT had F1 scores of 0.794 (with batch effects)
vs. 0.756 (after correction), and Geneformer scored 0.751 vs. 0.700. Overall, these results suggest that
foundation models tend to capture biologically meaningful features that are relatively robust to batch-specific
variation, supporting the validity of our benchmarking results.
5. Inadequate validation. "Validation collection" uses same data sources (GEO) as primary data. Independent
clinical cohorts (e.g., fresh biopsies, PDX models) are absent.
Response: Thanks for the comments. We would like to clarify that our original validation collection already
included independent clinical cohorts, specifically two PDX datasets (Data1 and Data2), three fresh biopsy
datasets (Data11, Data12, and Data17), and two organoid datasets (Data13 and Data14), as indicated in the
“Source” and “Tissue” columns of Supplementary Table 1. In addition, tumor tissues in this collection are
also derived from fresh biopsies, as documented in their original publications. Although all datasets were
obtained from GEO, they are derived from different published studies and generated at different times. These
differences are important, as they ensure broader biological and technical diversity and provide a stronger
basis for independent validation.
To further strengthen the validation across tissue types and sources, we expanded the validation
collection by retrieving seven additional fresh biopsy datasets (Data18–Data24). These represent the most
recent and comprehensive fresh biopsy data available in GEO, thereby maximizing the biological and
technical diversity of our validation resource. The external validation collection now comprises 24 datasets,
including 10 fresh biopsies, 2 PDX datasets, 2 organoid datasets, and 10 cell line datasets (Fig. 1;
Supplementary Table 2).
After quality control, the validation collection contains a total of 168,486 cells, of which 80,237
(47.62%) are sensitive cells and 88,249 (52.38%) are resistant cells according to the ground truth labels
(Supplementary Table 2). When stratified by data type, 8 out of 14 categories are approximately balanced
between sensitive and resistant cells. These include organoid, tumor tissue, colon cancer, NSCLC, pancreatic
cancer, chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and targeted therapy (Fig. 1d; Supplementary Table 2). Using these
curated data, we evaluated the performance of foundation models using layer-freezing. Model performance
was assessed across tissue types, drug classes, and cancer types. We have updated the abstract (line 22), the
“Model Evaluation in the Validation Data Collection” in Results section (lines 278-297), and the “Data
collection and preprocessing” in Methods (line 551), to include the details of this expanded validation dataset
and the corresponding evaluation results (Fig. 6; Supplementary Fig. 4).
Specifically, by data source (including fresh biopsy, PDX, organoid, and cell line), our results showed that
scFoundation consistently achieved the best performance across all four tissue types, with mean F1 scores of
0.932 (fresh biopsy), 0.926 (PDX), 0.973 (organoid), and 0.901 (cell line) (Supplementary Note 8;
Supplementary Fig. 21). Additionally, CellPLM, scGPT, and tGPT achieved strong performance specifically
on organoid data, with mean F1 scores of 0.900, 0.928, and 0.946, respectively. In addition, based on F1 score
and recall, we observed that the models generally performed worse in PDX data compared to the remaining
three tissue types, while other metrics including accuracy, AUROC, and precision did not vary much across
the four tissue types. This could be due to class imbalance, i.e., in the two PDX datasets, resistant cells
accounted for 72.2% and 57.54% of cells, respectively, which likely skewed the models toward under-
predicting the minority class (sensitive cells). Beyond imbalance, intrinsic biological features of PDX models
may also introduce additional complexity and noise, leading to reduced generalizability.
6. Methodological opacity. Preprocessing: Gene/cell QC thresholds (e.g., mitochondrial content) undefined;
LoRA tuning: Rank=8 used universally without ablation study; Prompt engineering: GPT4o-mini’s poor
performance may stem from suboptimal design (only top 10 genes input).
Response: Thanks for the comments. We have revised the manuscript to improve methodological clarity and
conducted additional analyses to strengthen our conclusions.
1) Regarding preprocessing, we have now explicitly described the steps in the “Data Collection and
Preprocessing” section in Methods (lines 554-558. Briefly, preprocessing of scRNA-seq data was performed
by Seurat (v4.3.0). Cells were retained if they had at least 500 detected genes (nFeature_RNA > 500) and
mitochondrial content (percent.mt) < 10%, ensuring removal of low-quality cells and technical artifacts.
Dimensionality reduction was performed using the top 30 principal components (PCs), and clustering was
conducted at a resolution of 0.5. These clarifications ensure transparency and reproducibility of our
preprocessing pipeline.
2) Regarding LoRA tuning, we agree that using rank=8 universally without ablation left room for
improvement. To address this, we conducted additional experiments with LoRA ranks of 4 and 16
(Supplementary Note 10, Supplementary Figs. 23-24). Overall, performance differences across ranks were
modest in both pooled-data and cross-data evaluations but some noteworthy exceptions emerged. For example,
in pooled-data evaluation (Supplementary Fig. 23), scFoundation fine-tuned with a LoRA rank of 8 achieved
significantly better predictive performance in liver and pancreatic cancers compared to the same model fine-
tuned with rank of 4 and 16. Specifically, in liver cancer, LoRA 8 significantly outperformed both LoRA 4 (p
= 0.0164) and LoRA 16 (p = 0.0086), while in pancreatic cancer, LoRA 8 outperformed LoRA 4 (p = 0.0104)
but not LoRA 16 (p > 0.05). Additionally, several other models fine-tuned with LoRA rank 8 also showed
improved performance over ranks 4 and 16 in specific contexts, even though these differences were not
statistically significant. Notable examples include UCE and Geneformer in acute myeloid leukemia, UCE in
tumor tissue, scBERT in immunotherapy, and both CellLM and Geneformer in targeted therapy. These
findings suggest that while LoRA rank influences fine-tuning performance in some pooled-data contexts, its
impact on generalization across heterogeneous datasets is limited. Importantly, they highlight that LoRA rank
8 provides a good balance between adaptability and efficiency.
In addition, under cross-dataset evaluation (Supplementary Fig. 24), none of the performance
differences across LoRA ranks reached statistical significance. Nonetheless, models fine-tuned with LoRA
rank 8 often performed better than those with ranks 4 or 16 in certain settings. For example, scFoundation in
tumor tissue, bone marrow aspirate, scBERT in PBMCs and multiple myeloma, UCE for breast cancer and
lung cancer, Geneformer and scBERT for prostate cancer, and scGPT for melanoma. This indicates that while
LoRA rank can influence fine-tuning outcomes in specific contexts, its overall effect on generalization
performance appears limited. Together, these results imply that moderate LoRA configurations may be
preferable in pooled-data scenarios, but LoRA rank selection may be less critical when prioritizing model
robustness across heterogeneous datasets.
3) Regarding prompt engineering for GPT4o-mini, we investigated alternative prompt templates to test
whether its suboptimal performance was due to design. In our revision, we compared three prompts: (1) the
top 10 highly expressed genes + data source, (2) the top 100 genes + data source, and (3) a chain-of-thought (CoT)
prompt designed to explicitly structure input and reasoning (Supplementary Note 7; Supplementary
Fig. 20). Across tissues, drugs, and cancer types, both the 10-gene and 100-gene prompts yielded comparable
F1 performance (e.g., tumor tissue: 0.519 vs. 0.506; PBMCs: 0.583 vs. 0.565). Interestingly, the 10-gene
prompt slightly outperformed the 100-gene prompt in multiple cancer types (e.g., lung, breast, CLL, prostate).
In contrast, the CoT prompt consistently underperformed in F1 scores, though it achieved higher accuracy in
select settings (e.g., immunotherapy, lung, MM, prostate). These results suggest that using a simple top-10-
gene prompt is at least as effective as, and often better than, a more complex 100-gene prompt. While GPT4o-
mini remains suboptimal overall, often performing close to or below baseline, the results indicate that prompt
design was not the primary factor driving its poor performance.
In summary, we have clarified our preprocessing criteria, expanded our LoRA rank evaluation, and tested
alternative prompt strategies. Together, these efforts address methodological opacity and reinforce the
robustness of our conclusions that while LoRA rank and prompt design can influence performance in specific
cases, the overall trends and comparative benchmarking results across foundation models remain consistent.
7. Authors used four evaluation metrics (F1, AUROC, precision, and recall) for assessing model performance
in predicting cell-level drug response. However, relying solely on these metrics may not provide a sufficiently
rigorous basis for model comparison. It is recommended to add statistical tests (e.g., p-values, confidence
intervals) to determine whether the performance differences between models are significant.
Response: Thanks for the comments. In this revision, we have added comparisons of model performance
across tissue types, drug types, and cancer types using Student’s t-test (Supplementary Note 1;
Supplementary Fig. 5; Supplementary Table 4). In the pooled-data evaluation, we compared the mean F1
score of each model to scFoundation, which was the best-performing model in this setting. In the cross-data
evaluation, we used scGPT as the reference model, as it demonstrated superior performance in tumor tissue.
Overall, in the pooled-data evaluation, under both layer-freezing and full fine-tuning settings, scFoundation
significantly outperformed all other models across different tissue, drug, and cancer types (Supplementary
Fig. 5; Supplementary Table 4). In contrast, under the cross-dataset evaluation, scGPT achieved significantly
better performance than LLaMa3 and tGPT in tumor tissue under the zero-shot setting. We also observed
several models that significantly outperformed scGPT in certain context (Supplementary Fig. 6;
Supplementary Table 4). For example, using layer-freezing training method, LLaMa3 was superior than
scGPT in both cell line and PBMCs (p-values, cell line: 0.0006; PBMCs: 0.0187), and tGPT also surpassed
scGPT in PBMCs (p-value: 0.0439). In addition, scFoundation and LLaMa3 outperformed scGPT in targeted
therapy (p-values, scFoundation: 0.0076; LLaMa3: <0.0001). Using fine-tuning training method, tGPT again
showed significantly better performance than scGPT in PBMCs (p = 0.0415). CellPLM and scFoundation
outperformed scGPT in targeted therapy (p-values, CellPLM: 0.04827; scFoundation: 0.0161). These findings
suggest that scFoundation is the most robust choice in pooled-data scenarios, whereas alternative models may
offer advantages in certain data types or therapeutic contexts under cross-data evaluation.
8. In the "Few-shot learning for drug response prediction" section, the evaluation of few-shot/zero-shot
learning is relatively brief, without a comprehensive analysis, for instance, of whether different prompt
templates influence prediction performance. Furthermore, the lack of comparison with similar methods makes
it difficult to assess the potential or limitations of large language models in drug response prediction.
Response: Thanks for the comments. In the revised manuscript, we have expanded both the prompt evaluation
and baseline comparisons to address these concerns.
1) As outlined in our response to comment #6, we systematically evaluated the impact of different prompt
templates on GPT4o-mini’s performance. Specifically, we tested three prompt types: (1) the top 10 most
highly expressed genes per cell along with the dataset source (e.g., GEO accession); (2) the top 100 genes
with dataset source; and (3) a chain-of-thought (CoT) prompt that explicitly defines the nested data structure
of cells and their expressed genes to guide reasoning. This enables the model to follow a predetermined order
when assessing drug sensitivity for each cell, helping to reduce ambiguity, improve the clarity and accuracy
of reasoning, and enhance result consistency and interpretability. Our results showed that the top-10 gene
prompt performed similarly to or slightly better than the 100-gene prompt across diverse tissue, drug, and
cancer types, while the COT prompt underperformed in all scenarios (Supplementary Note 7;
Supplementary Fig. 20). Importantly, we note that regardless of prompt design, GPT4o-mini’s overall drug
response prediction performance remained suboptimal, often close to or below baseline, highlighting its
current limitations for this task (Supplementary Note 7; Supplementary Fig. 20).
2) To evaluate whether foundation models (FMs) outperform similar traditional (non-FM) methods in drug
response prediction, we compared their performances with that of the multilayer perceptron (MLP), scDEAL
(a deep-learning model for cancer drug response prediction at single-cell level), and DREEP (a statistical
method for drug response estimation from single-cell transcriptional profiles of tumors). All these three
methods were assessed in pooled-data and cross-data scenarios (Supplementary Note 3; Supplementary Fig.
11-12).
Our results show that, overall, non-FM methods did not outperform foundation models. Interestingly, among
the non-FMs, the MLP trained on pooled data achieved strong and consistent results than scDEAL and DREEP
in several contexts, including targeted therapy, cell line data, and cancer datasets such as melanoma (F1 =
0.875 ± 0.0014), breast cancer (0.774 ± 0.0038), and lung cancer (0.737 ± 0.0041). In some cases, such as
liver cancer, scDEAL, DREEP, and MLP achieved performance equivalent to several foundation models (e.g.,
mean F1 = 0.924). However, across the broader evaluation landscape, particularly in cross-dataset scenarios
where generalization is critical, foundation models consistently demonstrated superior predictive power
compared with non-FMs. This highlights one of the central advantages of pre-trained FMs, i.e., their ability
to transfer learned representations and maintain performance across heterogeneous datasets, which is
especially important for drug response prediction in diverse cancer contexts. In summary, while non-FM
baselines can occasionally perform well under pooled-data conditions, our systematic comparisons show that
foundation models provide more robust and generalizable predictive performance, thereby reinforcing their
value for single-cell drug response prediction.
9. The manuscript lacks a thorough analysis of biological mechanisms behind model's prediction, whether the
model’s decisions depend on key genes, cell subpopulations, drug mechanisms, or other biological features.
Response: Thanks for the comment. In the revised manuscript, we added analyses to examine the biological
mechanisms underlying model’s predictions, including contributions from key genes, cell-cell interactions,
and drug-related pathways. To do this, we used Data 3 from the primary collection (Supplementary Tables
1–2) and compared downstream analyses based on ground-truth labels versus scGPT-predicted labels
(Supplementary Note 5; Supplementary Figs. 14–17).
According to ground-truth annotations, Data 3 contained 10,897 resistant tumor cells (67.95%) and 5,140
sensitive tumor cells (32.05%), whereas scGPT predicted a slightly shifted distribution (62.95% resistant vs.
37.05% sensitive). After QC, 35,870 cells were retained and analyzed with Seurat, yielding major populations
including 16,037 tumor cells, 4,923 CD8⁺ T cells, 1,157 CD4⁺ T cells, 6,077 monocytes/macrophages, 3,355
NK cells, 519 dendritic cells, 325 progenitors, 360 erythrocytes, and 3,117 B cells (Supplementary Fig. 14).
We then performed a series of downstream analyses, including differential expression, pathway enrichment
(GO, KEGG, MSigDB Hallmark), cell-cell communication, and pseudotime trajectory inference, to assess
key biological insights playing roles in model predictions. Using ground-truth labels, we identified key
resistance-associated genes (e.g., COL1A2, SEZ6L2), enriched pathways central to tumor biology and drug
resistance (e.g., cell differentiation, adhesion, p53 signaling), and clear intercellular communication patterns
(including stronger signaling to DCs and B cells and weakened BTLA/CD160 interactions in CD8⁺ T, NK,
and DC populations). Ground-truth labels also yielded a coherent pseudotime trajectory from sensitive to
resistant states (Supplementary Figs. 15–17). In contrast, some of these features were absent or attenuated
when using scGPT-predicted labels, suggesting that these biological signals may indeed inform model
predictions, but can be obscured when predictions are less accurate.
Taken together, this case study shows that foundation models can reflect underlying biology, including gene
expression, cell states, and drug mechanisms, but only when their predictions are sufficiently accurate. This
underscores the importance of ensuring accurate drug response prediction in single-cell studies to derive
reliable mechanistic insights.
Minor Concerns:
1. The study omits critical evaluation of technical confounders, including sequencing platform variability,
read depth heterogeneity, and batch effect correction methodologies. This analytical gap precludes definitive
attribution of performance differences to model capability versus data artifacts, thereby limiting assessment
of real-world applicability.
Response: Thanks for the comments. We have added the following analyses to address the comments:
1) Regarding sequencing platform variability, in our revised manuscript, we explicitly examined model
performance across six distinct platforms represented in our primary data collection: 10x Genomics (n=27),
BD Rhapsody (n=3), MARS-seq v2.0 (n=2), DropSeq (n=2), inDrop v3 (n=1), and SMART-seq v4 (n=1)
(Supplementary Table 1). Both layer-freezing and fine-tuning with LoRA were evaluated. Our results
showed that scFoundation consistently achieved the best performance across all protocols based on F1 scores.
For example, under layer-freezing training, scFoundation achieved mean F1 scores of 0.989 in BD Rhapsody,
0.963 in MARS-seq v2.0, 0.975 in 10x Genomics, 0.952 in DropSeq, 0.937 in inDrop v3, and 0.916 in
SMART-seq v4. Other metrics such as AUROC and accuracy also supported these findings (Supplementary
Note 6; Supplementary Fig. 19a). Under fine-tuning, we observed a similar pattern where scFoundation
remained the best-performing model across all protocols (F1 scores: BD Rhapsody: 1.000; MARS-seq v2.0: 0.989;
10x Genomics: 0.958; DropSeq: 0.893; inDrop v3: 0.749; SMART-seq v4: 0.654). Notably, fine-tuning
improved performance for BD Rhapsody and MARS-seq v2.0 datasets by 1.1% and 2.6%, respectively, but
decreased performance for the other four protocols (10x Genomics: -1.7%, DropSeq: -5.9%, inDrop v3: -
18.8%, SMART-seq v4: -26.2%). This suggests that fine-tuning can enhance model adaptation to certain
protocols but may introduce overfitting or reduce robustness in others. Additionally, Geneformer consistently
ranked as the second-best model in five out of six protocols, highlighting some stability in its cross-protocol
generalization, though all models struggled with inDrop v3 and SMART-seq v4 (Supplementary Note 6;
Supplementary Fig. 19b).
2) Regarding read depth heterogeneity, our investigation into the effect of read depth on foundation model
performance is constrained by data availability. Our curated scDrugMap datasets are predominantly sourced
from NCBI GEO, where raw sequencing files and standardized per-cell QC metrics (e.g., true read depth) are
rarely available. While some datasets mention sequencing depth in their original publications, their provided
expression matrices do not provide measures of read depth. Consequently, in the absence of standardized per-
cell QC metrics or raw sequencing files, it is not feasible to systematically evaluate read depth effects across
our diverse dataset collection.
3) Regarding batch effects, we applied Harmony on the top 2000 highly variable genes in each dataset to
correct batch effects (Supplementary Note 2; Supplementary Figs. 7-8). With the batch corrected data, we
then conducted comprehensive benchmarking under two evaluation scenarios: pooled-data evaluation
(Supplementary Fig. 7) and cross-data evaluation (Supplementary Fig. 8). In both scenarios, we also
implemented two model training strategies (layer freezing and fine-tuning using LoRA). Our results showed
that performance with batch correction was largely consistent with the results obtained without correction.
Top-performing models such as scFoundation, scGPT, and CellPLM remained stable or exhibited only minor
improvements after batch correction (Supplementary Fig. 7a). For example, in tumor tissue, the F1 scores
with and without batch correction were: scFoundation = 0.998 vs. 0.998; scGPT = 0.939 vs. 0.939; and
CellPLM = 0.940 vs. 0.936. This phenomenon is also observed in other models, such as tGPT, Geneformer,
and UCE, exhibited comparable performance before and after batch correction. For instance, in targeted
therapy datasets, tGPT had F1 scores of 0.794 (with batch effects) vs. 0.756 (after correction), and Geneformer
scored 0.751 vs. 0.700. Overall, these results suggest that foundation models tend to capture biologically
meaningful features that are relatively robust to batch-specific variation, supporting the validity of our
benchmarking results.
2. The manuscript contains spelling errors (such as "cance", "componennts"), inappropriate phrasing (e.g.,
"enhance limitation"). Additionally, some paragraphs contain repetitive sentence patterns, which should be
revised for conciseness and clarity.
Response: Thanks for the comments. We have carefully revised the manuscript to correct the identified errors.
Specifically, we corrected “cance” (line 121, “componennts” (line 481), and other typographical issues, such
as the PBMCs acronym in line 152. The phrase “enhance limitation” has been corrected to “mitigate limitation”
(line 441), and the redundant use of “layer” in line 162 has been removed. We also reviewed the manuscript
more broadly to improve conciseness, reduce repetitive sentence patterns, and enhance overall clarity.
3. Several figures show missing or unclear information. In Fig.1 and Fig.6, legends are incomplete (e.g.,
unclear what color shades or line colors represent). Fig.2 and Fig.3 lack stylistic consistency and statistical
significance markers. In Fig.4c, the UCE group fails to distinguish between resistant and sensitive cells.
Response: Thanks for the comments. We have revised the figures to address these issues:
1) For Fig. 1c and Fig. 1d, we updated the legend to clarify the meaning of color shades (lines 597-600).
Darker shades now denote the number of sensitive cells, while lighter shades represent the number of resistant
cells.
2) In Fig. 6, we added a complete legend to explain the line colors (lines 631-633), with each color
corresponding to a specific category within the data type.
3) For Fig. 2 and Fig. 3, we improved stylistic consistency and added statistical significance assessments.
Statistical comparisons are now presented in Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6, with exact p-values provided in
Supplementary Table 4 and detailed explanations in Supplementary Note 1. Briefly, we used Student’s t-
tests to evaluate performance across tissue types, drug classes, and cancer types. In pooled-data settings,
scFoundation consistently outperformed other models under both layer-freezing and fine-tuning strategies. In
cross-dataset evaluations, results were more context-specific: for example, LLaMa3 outperformed scGPT in
cell line and PBMC datasets under layer-freezing, while tGPT surpassed scGPT in PBMCs under both layer-
freezing and fine-tuning. These findings indicate that scFoundation remains the most robust in pooled-data
contexts, whereas alternative models may offer advantages in specific cross-dataset scenarios.
4) For Fig. 3a, we replaced the violin plot with a box plot to ensure stylistic consistency with Fig. 3b.
5) For Fig. 4c, we acknowledge that UCE fails to distinguish resistant from sensitive cells. To avoid
misinterpretation, we removed the corresponding text and added the UMAP visualization of all other methods
in Supplementary Fig. 18.
4. Line 102 contains an incorrect attribution to scFoundation.
Response: Thanks for the comments. We have corrected the citation from #16 to #15 (line 102).
5. In Figure 1C-D, the 'Number of cells' bar charts employ graduated color shading within categorical
segments (e.g., tissue/drug/cancer types). The manuscript does not define what these intensity variations
represent—whether hierarchical substructures, response status distributions, or data source heterogeneity.
Clarification should be provided in the figure legend or methods to ensure interpretability.
Response: Thanks for the comments. As clarified in our response to Comment #3, we have revised the legends
for Fig. 1c and Fig. 1d to explicitly define the meaning of the color shades (lines 597–600). Specifically,
darker shades represent the number of sensitive cells, while lighter shades represent the number of resistant
cells. To provide additional context, the primary data collection comprises 36 scRNA-seq datasets with a total
of 326,751 single tumor cells, including 162,957 (49.87%) sensitive and 162,794 (50.13%) resistant cells
(Supplementary Table 2). The validation collection consists of 24 datasets with 168,486 cells, including
80,237 (47.62%) sensitive and 88,249 (52.38%) resistant cells (Supplementary Table 2). These clarifications
ensure that the meaning of the shading is transparent and that the bar charts in Fig. 1c–d can be accurately
interpreted.
Web server Concerns:
1. The "README" part is insufficient and requires clear, step-by-step instructions for using the tool.
Response: Thanks for the comments. We have substantially revised the README section to provide clear,
step-by-step guidance for users. The updated instructions now walk through the full workflow, including
model selection, input file requirements, data upload and preprocessing, prediction modes (fixed embeddings
and fine-tuning), and downloading results. To improve usability, we also added a downloadable example input
file and clarified the expected format for gene expression matrices, including cell barcodes, condition labels,
and gene counts. The README now explains adjustable training parameters and shows how progress and
metrics are displayed in real time. These updates make the README far more comprehensive, ensuring users
can easily follow the workflow and successfully run scDrugMap without coding expertise.
2. In the "Tool" section, users can upload all input CSV files. It would be helpful to provide a sample file to
clarify the expected forma.
Response: Thanks for the comments. We agree that providing a sample input file will greatly help users
understand the expected format. In the revised web server, we have added a downloadable sample CSV file
in the “Tool” section. This example includes the required column names, data types, and example entries,
clearly demonstrating how input data should be structured. We have also updated the README/user guide to
explain the meaning of each column and any formatting requirements (e.g., gene names, cell ID). Together,
these additions will make it much easier for users to prepare their own input files and avoid formatting errors.
3. Some single-cell drug resistance datasets are available for download in "Data" section. To improve
interpretability, visual summaries (UMAP/t-SNE) are recommended. Also, the download button beside the
dataset is currently not working.
Response: Thanks for the comments. We have addressed both issues in the revised web server. First, to
improve interpretability, we added visual summaries (UMAP/t-SNE plots) for each dataset in the “Data”
section. These plots provide users with an overview of the cellular heterogeneity and resistance versus
sensitivity distribution in each dataset, making it easier to understand the data before downloading. Second,
we fixed the download functionality so that the download button beside each dataset is now fully operational.
Users can now directly access and download the datasets without technical issues. These improvements
enhance both usability and interpretability of the “Data” section.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
The manuscript presents scDrugMap, a benchmarking framework evaluating large foundation models for
single-cell drug response prediction. Here are the detailed comments:
1. While the paper appropriately notes that accuracy is suitable for balanced data (lines 502-503) and confirms
the drug sensitivity/resistance data is balanced (lines 119-121, 129-130), there appears to be an inconsistency
as F1 scores (more appropriate for imbalanced data, lines 503-504) are predominantly reported. Furthermore,
although accuracy is repeatedly mentioned as being tested (lines 143-145, 160-161, 240-242), the results
figures lack this metric, creating a discrepancy with the Results section.
Response: Thanks for the comments. To address this, we have now included accuracy plots in
Supplementary Figures 1–4, alongside the F1 scores. Overall, we find that models with strong F1 scores also
achieve correspondingly high accuracy, supporting consistency across metrics. Below we provide detailed
results:
1) In the pooled-data evaluation using layer-freezing training method, scFoundation, scGPT, and CellPLM
achieved the highest mean F1 scores, 0.998, 0.939, and 0.939, respectively, and also ranked as the top three
in accuracy, with 0.997 for scFoundation, 0.923 for scGPT, and 0.923 for CellPLM. In contrast, the lowest-
performing models were scBERT (F1: 0.789, Accuracy: 0.725), LLaMa3 (F1: 0.760, Accuracy: 0.728), and
CellLM (F1: 0.749, Accuracy: 0.679) (Fig. 2a; Supplementary Fig. 1a).
2) In the pooled-data evaluation using fine-tuning training method, scFoundation, scGPT, and CellPLM
achieved the highest mean F1 scores, 0.990, 0.963, and 0.959, respectively, and also ranked as the top three
in accuracy, with 0.987 for scFoundation, 0.954 for scGPT, and 0.948 for CellPLM. UCE (F1: 0.869,
Accuracy: 0.838), CellLM (F1: 0.732, Accuracy: 0.676), and scBERT (F1: 0.708, Accuracy: 0.655) (Fig. 2b;
Supplementary Fig. 1b).
3) In the cross-data evaluation using layer-freezing training method, scGPT was the only model that performed
well, achieving the highest mean F1 score (0.858) and the highest accuracy (0.590), although the accuracy
was only slightly above baseline (Fig. 3a; Supplementary Fig. 2a).
4) In the cross-data evaluation using fine-tuning training method, UCE and Geneformer achieved the highest
F1 scores (0.774 and 0.701, respectively), indicating relatively good but not outstanding performance. In terms
of accuracy, however, CellLM ranked first (0.816), while UCE (0.739) and Geneformer (0.749) were in the
middle range. This discrepancy between F1 score and accuracy emphasize the needs to report comprehensive
metrics to evaluate model performances, especially when data are unbalanced (Fig. 3b; Supplementary Fig.
2b).
5) To complement the five metrics reported, we further assessed area under the precision–recall curve
(AUPRC) on datasets with resistant-class prevalence >70% (Data 23: 84.49% resistant; Data 32: 79.85%
resistant; Supplementary Table 2). All models exceeded baseline AUPRC. Pooled-data training consistently
outperformed cross-data training. For example, in pooled-data scenario, for Data 23, scFoundation, scGPT,
and CellPLM achieved AUPRC >0.7. For Data 32, scFoundation, scGPT, and CellPLM also outperformed
others (Supplementary Note 9; Supplementary Fig. 22).
In summary, we have clarified this inconsistency by adding accuracy plots and providing complementary
AUPRC analyses for unbalanced settings. Together, these results demonstrate that models performing well by
F1 generally also perform well by accuracy, and that pooled-data evaluation yields consistently stronger
performance under class imbalance.
2. While the paper provides a comprehensive comparison of model performance across various scenarios
using metrics like F1, the underlying reasons for the observed performance differences (e.g., pretraining
strategy, model architecture, or dataset characteristics) remain unexplored; a deeper analysis of these factors
would significantly strengthen the mechanistic understanding of why certain models outperform others in
specific contexts, ultimately providing more actionable insights for readers seeking to select or develop
appropriate models for their applications.
Response: Thanks for the comments. We agree that exploring the underlying reasons behind the observed
performance differences can provide important mechanistic insights. To address this, we conducted an in-
depth analysis across all compared models (tGPT, scBERT, Geneformer, CellLM, scFoundation, scGPT,
CellPLM, UCE, LLaMA3-7B, and GPT-4), and the results are summarized in Supplementary Table 6.
Our benchmarking results show that scFoundation achieved the best overall performance, may primarily due
to its domain-specific, large-scale pretraining on single-cell transcriptomic data, which allows it to capture
fine-grained gene–gene interactions and cell-state relationships. scGPT and UCE also performed well, likely
benefiting from specialized architectures and training corpora that integrate biological priors and task-specific
objectives. In contrast, scBERT and CellLM showed lower performance, which may due to their pretraining
datasets that were smaller and less diverse, limiting generalization to our test scenarios. GPT-4 ranked lowest,
consistent with its general-purpose design, while highly capable in natural language processing, it lacks
exposure to structured biological expression data and domain-specific vocabulary during pretraining, resulting
in weaker performance in this specialized task.
Overall, these results suggest that performance in single-cell drug response prediction tasks is strongly
influenced by three factors: (1) the domain relevance of pretraining data, (2) the scale of pretraining datasets,
and (3) the architectural design of the models. Models specifically pre-trained on large-scale single-cell
transcriptomic data (such as scFoundation, scGPT, and UCE) consistently perform well, offering broad
coverage of cell types and states while effectively capturing complex gene-gene and cell-state relationships
through biologically informed vocabularies or multi-omics fusion strategies. By comparison, although
Geneformer possesses strong embedding capabilities, its lack of specialization for single-cell heterogeneity
leads to slightly lower performance than these domain-optimized models. Models trained on smaller or less
diverse datasets (such as CellPLM, scBERT, and CellLM) face significant generalization challenges,
especially when applied to unseen cell types or conditions. For general-purpose large language models (such
as LLaMA3-7B and GPT-4), the absence of pretraining directly related to gene expression and single-cell
biology results in markedly lower performance, underscoring the critical role of domain-specific knowledge
in bioinformatics prediction tasks.
In addition to Supplementary Table 6, we have now included a Model Recommendation Guide
(Supplementary Table 5), which outlines the optimal scLLMs for each data type across four evaluation
scenarios: (1) pooled-data with layer-freezing, (2) pooled-data with fine-tuning, (3) cross-data with layer-
freezing, and (4) cross-data with fine-tuning. We hope this guide provides readers with actionable insights for
selecting or developing models most appropriate for their specific tissue, cancer type, or drug-response
application.
3. The statement that "other models showed limited separation" in Fig. 4 would be more informative if
accompanied by corresponding UMAP visualizations of these underperforming models, as this would enable
readers to directly compare the separation quality across all evaluated methods and better understand the
performance differences.
Response: Thanks for the comments. To address this, we have added the UMAP visualizations for all the rest
models in Supplementary Fig. 18. In details, Fig. 4 showed the two models (scFoundation and scGPT) that
performed well in most of the datasets and sceniros. These visualizations revealed that scFoundation and
scGPT effectively distinguished drug-resistant and drug-sensitive cells. However, the UMAP visualizations
other models in Supplementary Fig. 18 showed limited separation between resistant and sensitive tumor cells.
These additional plots allow readers to directly compare separation quality across all methods and better
appreciate the performance differences.
4. The choice of LoRA rank=8 lacks justification. A brief ablation study (e.g., testing ranks 4/8/16) would
strengthen the methodology.
Response: Thanks for the comments. We have conducted additional analyses using LoRA ranks of 4 and 16
to complement the original rank 8 setting, as detailed in Supplementary Note 10 and mentioned in the
Methods section. Overall, performance differences across ranks were modest in both pooled-data and cross-
dataset evaluations. However, some notable exceptions emerged. In the pooled-data evaluation
(Supplementary Fig. 23), we found that scFoundation fine-tuned with a LoRA rank of 8 achieved
significantly better predictive performance in liver and pancreatic cancers compared to the same model fine-
tuned with ranks 4 and 16. Specifically, in liver cancer, LoRA 8 significantly outperformed both LoRA 4 (p
= 0.0164) and LoRA 16 (p = 0.0086), while in pancreatic cancer, LoRA 8 outperformed LoRA 4 (p = 0.0104)
but not LoRA 16 (p > 0.05). Additionally, several other models fine-tuned with LoRA rank 8 showed
improved performance over ranks 4 and 16 in specific contexts, even though these differences were not
statistically significant. Notable examples include UCE and Geneformer in acute myeloid leukemia, UCE in
tumor tissue, scBERT in immunotherapy, and both CellLM and Geneformer in targeted therapy. These
findings suggest that an intermediate LoRA rank (e.g., 8) may offer a favourable balance between model
adaptability and parameter efficiency in certain cancer types.
By contrast, under cross-dataset evaluation (Supplementary Fig. 24), none of the performance
differences across LoRA ranks reached statistical significance. Nonetheless, models fine-tuned with LoRA
rank 8 often performed better than those with ranks 4 or 16 in certain settings. For example, scFoundation in
tumor tissue, bone marrow aspirate, scBERT in PBMCs and multiple myeloma, UCE for breast cancer and
lung cancer, Geneformer and scBERT for prostate cancer, and scGPT for melanoma. This indicates that while
LoRA rank can influence fine-tuning outcomes in specific contexts, its overall effect on generalization
performance appears limited within the tested range. Together, these results imply that moderate LoRA
configurations may be preferable in pooled-data scenarios, but LoRA rank selection may be less critical when
prioritizing model robustness across heterogeneous datasets.
5. Please add a summary table (e.g., "Model Recommendation Guide") to highlight optimal models for specific
scenarios (e.g., UCE for generalizability). This would improve practical utility.
Response: Thank you for the helpful suggestion. We have added a Model Recommendation Guide as
Supplementary Table 5, which summarizes the optimal scLLMs for each data type across four evaluation
scenarios: (1) pooled-data with layer-freezing, (2) pooled-data with fine-tuning, (3) cross-data with layer-
freezing, and (4) cross-data with fine-tuning.
To enhance interpretability, we defined performance thresholds for inclusion: 1) For pooled-data scenarios,
models with mean F1 ≥ 0.95 were considered optimal. For models with mean F1 between 0.5 and 0.95, we
additionally included the top-performing model (top 1) per subtask. 2) For cross-data scenarios, a more
conservative threshold of mean F1 ≥ 0.70 was used to account for the increased difficulty in generalization.
For models with mean F1 between 0.5 and 0.70, we included the top two performers (top 2) per subtask. These
cutoffs were selected based on the observed distribution of F1 scores across all tasks and aim to provide a
practical reference for researchers selecting models under different constraints.
Briefly, based on our benchmarking across tissues, drug types, and cancer types, we provide a Model
Recommendation Guide for selecting scLLMs for cancer drug resistance prediction task (Supplementary
Table 5). This guide summarizes the best-performing scLLMs across four evaluation settings: (1) pooled-data
with layer-freezing, (2) pooled-data with fine-tuning, (3) cross-data with layer-freezing, and (4) cross-data with
fine-tuning. By linking model performance to evaluation scenario, tissue type, drug class, and cancer
type, the guide offers a practical framework for selecting or adapting models to specific research contexts.
Overall, scFoundation and scGPT emerge as strong default choices for pooled-data applications across most
tissues, drug classes, and cancer types. In contrast, cross-data scenarios require more careful consideration, as
performance tends to be more variable. In these cases, models such as UCE, tGPT, and other task-specific
architectures often demonstrate stronger generalization. Finally, for rare cancers or highly imbalanced datasets,
we recommend that researchers place particular emphasis on cross-data performance, since not all models are
equally reliable under such challenging conditions.
6. The triplicate repetition of post-prompt in Fig. 5a appears redundant. Please clarify whether this design is
necessary.
Response: Thanks for the comments. The repeated post-prompts in Fig. 5a are intentional and serve as a
prompt engineering strategy to encourage the LLM to maintain a consistent output format. Repetition of
instructions or contextual cues has been shown in recent studies to improve model adherence to complex tasks
by reinforcing the desired behavior.
Our prompt design is inspired by Hou et.al.[1], which evaluated GPT4's performance on cell annotation, and
we adapted it to drug sensitivity tasks. Although Hou et.al.[1] did not explicitly employ repeated post-prompts,
in our experiments we found that repetition improved output stability, minimized formatting errors, and
reduced hallucinations. This observation is supported by the broader literature. For example, Kojima et al.
(2022)[2] demonstrated that “chain-of-thought” prompting, which involves repeated or stepwise guidance,
improves reasoning and instruction adherence in LLMs. Similarly, Wei et al. (2022)[3] found that providing
repeated contextual signals or exemplars can stabilize model outputs and reduce variability. Microsoft Azure
documentation[4] highlights that LLMs display a strong recency bias, they are particularly influenced by text
appearing at the end of the prompt. As a result, repeating instructions at the end can help the model retain
critical guidance that might otherwise be forgotten or overshadowed. Webson et.et.al.[5] compared the effects of
single-task and multi-task prompts, emphasized the impact of repeated prompt structure on the performance
of different tasks and models, and provided empirical support for the design of repeated prompt
comprehension prompts. Shaier et.al.[6] on prompt repetition in reading comprehension tasks found that
repeating a question multiple times within a prompt (e.g., 3 or 5 times) can improve model focus and
comprehension compared to single-instance presentations[7], suggesting that training a model through repeated
human feedback can enhance its ability to follow instructions. Therefore, the triple repetition of post-prompts
was deliberately applied to enhance robustness by reducing ambiguity and ensuring that the model consistently
produced outputs in the required format. This design choice aligns with recent advances in prompt engineering
aimed at better controlling large language model behavior.
References:
[1] Hou, W., & Ji, Z. (2024). Assessing GPT-4 for cell type annotation in single-cell RNA-seq analysis. Nature
methods, 21(8), 1462-1465.
[2] Kojima, T., Gu, S. S., Reid, M., Matsuo, Y., & Iwasawa, Y. (2022). Large language models are zero-shot
reasoners. Advances in neural information processing systems, 35, 22199-22213.
[3] Wei, J., Wang, X., Schuurmans, D., Le, Q., & others. (2022). Chain of Thought Prompting Elicits
Reasoning in Large Language Models. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 2022.
[4] Microsoft Azure AI. (2024). Prompt engineering techniques: Overcoming recency bias. Microsoft Learn
documentation. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-foundry/openai/concepts/prompt-engineering
[5] Webson, A., & Pavlick, E. (2022, July). Do prompt-based models really understand the meaning of their
prompts?. In Proceedings of the 2022 conference of the north american chapter of the association for
computational linguistics: Human language technologies (pp. 2300-2344).
[6] Shaier, S., Sanz-Guerrero, M., & von der Wense, K. (2024). Asking again and again: exploring LLM
robustness to repeated questions. arXiv preprint arXiv:2412.07923.
[7] Ouyang, L., Wu, J., Jiang, X., Almeida, D., Wainwright, C., Mishkin, P., ... & Lowe, R. (2022). Training
language models to follow instructions with human feedback. Advances in neural information processing
systems, 35, 27730-27744.
7. Several critical aspects of the web interface remain unclear, significantly limiting its usability and
reproducibility. Specifically: (1) The required format and structure of uploaded CSV files are not documented.
(2) The model selection and fine-tuning configuration interface lacks clarity—for example, whether users can
choose between freezing layers or enabling full fine-tuning. (3) There is no guidance on how to set key
parameters such as LoRA rank. (4) It is unclear how and where users can download the fine-tuned models. (5)
The functional distinction between the “LLM TOOLS” and “DATA BROWSER” tabs is ambiguous, as both
appear to redirect to the same “Data” page.
Response: Thanks for the comments. We have substantially revised the README and web interface
documentation to address each of the concerns raised:
1) Input file format: We added a downloadable sample CSV file in the “Tool” section that specifies required
column names, data types, and example entries. The README now explains how to structure input files (e.g.,
gene expression matrices with cell barcodes, condition labels, and gene counts) and provides formatting
requirements to prevent errors.
2) Model selection and fine-tuning configuration: The updated user guide now explicitly describes the options
for model selection, including whether to freeze layers or enable full fine-tuning. We also explain how to
configure prediction modes (fixed embeddings vs. fine-tuning) so users can make informed choices.
3) Training parameters (e.g., LoRA rank): We added adjustable parameters such as LoRA rank, with
recommended default values and guidance on how parameter choices may influence model performance
(Supplementary Note 10).
4) Downloading fine-tuned models: Instructions are now provided on where and how users can download
fine-tuned models after training. The interface also shows progress and evaluation metrics in real time to
improve transparency.
5) Distinction between “LLM TOOLS” and “DATA BROWSER”: We clarified the functional roles of each
tab in the user guide. “LLM TOOLS” is now described as the module for model-based prediction, while
“DATA BROWSER” is designated for uploaded datasets.
Together, these revisions ensure that users have step-by-step guidance through the full workflow, from input
file preparation to model configuration, training, and result download, making the platform more transparent,
reproducible, and user-friendly even for those without coding expertise.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks on code availability):
The provided code is accompanied by a well-written README, which is helpful for reproduction. To further
improve usability and ensure environment consistency, I suggest providing a Docker image or Dockerfile for
easier setup and deployment.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this constructive suggestion. We have created a Dockerfile that allows
users to easily set up and deploy the full environment. The Docker configuration specifies all required
dependencies and versions, ensuring reproducibility across systems. Instructions for building and running the
Docker image have been added to the GitHub README, alongside the existing installation guide. This
addition will make it simpler for users to deploy the tool in different computational environments.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: The authors have a done a great job in addressing my concerns.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors have revised the manuscript to respond to the reviewers’ initial feedback. These changes have greatly
enhanced the manuscript’s clarity, methodological rigor, and biological insights. However, several issues still remain,
including aspects such as novelty, clinical applicability, and reliability, as detailed below:
1．In clinical applications, scenarios are often closer to cross-data rather than pooled-data settings. Moreover, as reported in
the manuscript, most models achieve an F1< 0.8 in cross-data evaluations, which may indicate limited performance when
applied to truly independent datasets. The manuscript devotes substantial discussion to the high scores obtained under
pooled-data conditions, which could potentially mislead readers regarding the practical utility of the proposed models.
2．The comparison between foundation models and non-foundation models should be a crucial part of the paper, but both
its design and presentation are extremely weak. The only relevant materials, Supplementary Figs. 11–12, also have obvious
issues: when presenting the AUROC performance of MLP, scDEAL, and DREEP across different cancer types, the box plots
in the two figures are inconsistent. Furthermore, the comparison in Supplementary Note 3 relies entirely on the F1 score,
which is insufficient to support the conclusion.
3．In the Few-shot learning section, only one general-purpose language model, GPT4o-mini, was used. The poor
performance of GPT4o-mini may be due to its own characteristics ("lightweight model"). It is not possible to conclude that
"general-purpose language models lack the precision and robustness".
Minor Concerns:
1.“For datasets exhibiting batch effects, we used Harmony package to correct for them”, the key parameters for Harmony
were not specified, and the difference between the datasets before and after batch removal is not shown, it is uncertain
whether the model is genuinely immune to batch effects
2.Although the authors added fresh biopsy and PDX datasets, all the data still come from GEO, lacking completely
independent clinical data.
3.The manuscript reports using Seurat v4 for data preprocessing, retaining cells with nFeature RNA > 500 and percent.mt <
10%. However, it does not clarify whether preprocessing parameters were adjusted for different datasets (e.g., different
sequencing technologies or tissue sources). For example, percent.mt vary across different tissue types, the appropriateness
of applying a uniform filtering threshold requires further clarification.
4.In Supplementary Fig. 22, the authors show AUPRC results for imbalanced datasets. It looks like for most foundation
models, under both cross-data and pooled-data settings, the prediction performance is pretty poor (AUPRC < 0.7). This
really should be pointed out clearly in manuscript. Also, the y-axis scale in Supplementary Fig. 22 seems to have an issue.

Response: Thanks for the comments. We fully agree that real-world clinical applications are better reflected by
cross-data rather than pooled-data settings, where models are required to generalize across independent datasets
and experimental contexts. To address this, we thoroughly reviewed and revised the manuscript to ensure a clear
and balanced presentation of both pooled-data and cross-data findings. In particular, we strengthened the emphasis
on cross-data results, and explicitly discussed the limitations of cross-data performance to avoid any potential
misinterpretation of model utility in practical scenarios.
Specifically, we revised the Abstract section (page 1), Results section (page 6), Discussion section (page 10),
and Supplementary Note 3 to provide deeper quantitative analysis and interpretation of cross-data performance.
These revisions together ensure that the manuscript accurately conveys both the current limitations and future
potentials of foundation models, presenting a transparent and balanced discussion of their performance across
both pooled-data and cross-data scenarios.
The revised changes are shown as follows:
(Abstract, page 1): “In the cross-data scenario, UCE for tumor tissue showed relatively better performance (mean
F1 score of 0.774) after fine-tuning, while scGPT for tumor tissue showed the best performance (mean F1 score
of 0.858) in a zero-shot learning setting.”
(Results, page 6): “Given that cross-data evaluations better reflect real-world clinical applications, foundation
models typically show lower absolute F1 scores (generally below 0.8) under these more stringent conditions,
highlighting the inherent challenge of generalizing across heterogeneous datasets. Nevertheless, they consistently
outperform traditional architectures such as scDEAL, demonstrating greater robustness and transferability
(Supplementary Note 3). This indicates that cross-data evaluations provide a more realistic measure of clinical

limitations, emphasizing the need for future work to further enhance their generalizability and performance.”
(Discussion, page 10): “Additionally, our study highlighted that models in pooled-data evaluation outperformed
those in cross-data evaluation. This indicates that single-cell foundation models (FMs) benefit from exposure to
a broader range of data within a given category. When datasets from multiple studies within the same category
(e.g., tumor tissue) are pooled together, the broader diversity may allow the model to learn from heterogeneous
sources for more accurate prediction. In contrast, when training is performed on each dataset separately, the model
often struggles to generalize, as it is less able to apply its pre-trained knowledge to a narrower and more specific
context. Importantly, in cross-data evaluations, which more closely reflect real-world clinical conditions, most
models achieved F1 scores below 0.8, indicating that while single-cell FMs show promise, their practical utility
remains limited when applied to fully independent datasets. This underscores the need for continued
methodological innovation to enhance robustness and cross-study generalization.”
(Supplementary Note 3): “More importantly, when evaluated in cross-data scenarios, which test generalization
across unseen datasets, critical for real-world predictive modeling, foundation models demonstrated clear and
consistent superiority over all non-FMs. For example, in prostate cancer, MLP achieved F1 = 0.33, Accuracy =
